description: We're Edison Gonzalez and Sebastian Cetina, a two-person team, kind of a yin and yang. I love talking, thinking outside the box and selling ideas. Sebastian Cetina likes order and planning, so I bring the spark and he brings the structure. We're small on purpose, so everyone gets real say and real work. We're both systems engineering students and would love someone in data analysis, design/UX or who knows NASA data. Mostly, someone curious, motivated and easy to work with.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an offline-first 3D tool that helps mission planners, educators, and the public explore and compare lunar landing sites (Apollo, CLPS, other missions, Artemis polar candidates, and custom coordinates) for any date and time in UTC.

Using real NASA LRO LOLA elevation data and Astronomy Engine ephemerides, it builds the true local horizon of each site and shows the terrain with the Sun and Earth in the sky. Users can see solar elevation, Earth visibility, solar energy potential, and the longest periods of darkness and lost direct-to-Earth communication, compare alternative launch dates, and generate PDF reports, all computed on the device.

It addresses the challenge by turning complex lunar data into clear, comparable information for choosing a landing site. It works offline as a PWA and Android app in seven languages, and includes a learning zone with 27 lessons, an AI tutor, and 3D games, so anyone, even a child, can use it and learn.

Open NASA data made simple, accessible, and fun for everyone.
details:
PROJECT NAME
Lunar Landing Site Navigator

HIGH-LEVEL PROJECT SUMMARY
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an offline-first 3D tool that helps mission planners, educators, and the public explore and compare lunar landing sites (Apollo, CLPS, other missions, Artemis polar candidates, and custom coordinates) for any date and time in UTC. From the surface, it shows the real terrain and the position of the Sun and Earth, so users can quickly understand solar elevation, Earth visibility, energy potential, and direct-to-Earth communication windows. It also includes a learning section with lessons, an AI tutor, and classic-style games. It turns complex lunar data into something simple, accessible, and fun for everyone.

LINK TO PROJECT DEMO
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1b_mfmanaxidF2ck3V-C8lEsoGU6kfbyQ?usp=sharing
Presentation video: https://youtu.be/C9W78Iq69lQ?si=s1_QxNVZJN1QEm5Q

LINK TO FINAL PROJECT
https://github.com/Terminator2424/Lunar-Landing-Site-Navigator
(Live web app: https://lunar-site-navigator.expo.app)

DETAILED PROJECT DESCRIPTION

What it does: Lets users pick a landing site on a 3D lunar globe or by coordinates, choose a date and time, and look at the surface with the Earth in the sky. For each site it computes the percentage of time with Sunlight and Earth visibility, the longest periods of darkness and of lost communication, upcoming sunrise/sunset and Earth rise/set events, and estimated solar energy for four panel configurations. It compares alternative launch dates (+1 day up to +1 year), shows side-by-side 3D terrain comparisons, and generates per-site PDF reports on the device.

How it works: It combines real lunar topography and imagery with ephemerides of the Sun, Earth, and Moon calculated by UTC date. For every site, a 360° horizon mask is built from LRO LOLA elevation models (including lunar curvature), so shadows and visibility reflect the real relief rather than an ideal sphere. For custom coordinates, the app downloads only the needed bytes of the NASA LOLA maps using HTTP range requests and builds the terrain and horizon on the device. All calculations run locally, with no server of our own.

Benefits: Works offline as a PWA and as an Android app, in seven languages (Spanish, English, Portuguese, French, German, Chinese, Japanese), and on web, Android, and desktop. It is designed so that even a child can use it and learn, with an educational zone of 27 lessons, an AI tutor, and 3D games.

Tools: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS; Three.js (3D graphics, Draco), cannon-es (game physics), astronomy-engine (ephemerides), jsPDF (reports), Vite (bundling), vite-plugin-pwa/Workbox (offline PWA), Capacitor (Android app), Google Gemini API (AI tutor), EAS Hosting (Expo) for deployment, Node.js, and puppeteer for automated tests.

NASA DATA
We used NASA LRO LOLA topography data (Planetary Data System, PDS Geosciences Node) for the terrain of the Moon and the landing sites, and LROC WAC imagery (LRO WAC mosaic and LROC QuickMap links) plus the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio CGI Moon Kit for the lunar surface texture. We also used NASA 3D Resources models for lessons and games.

SPACE AGENCY PARTNER & OTHER DATA
Astronomy Engine by Don Cross, MIT license (ephemerides of the Sun, Earth, and Moon by UTC date); Solar System Scope textures (CC BY 4.0) for Earth and the starry sky; Google Gemini API for the AI tutor.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
We used AI tools, mainly Kiro and Claude, to generate the audio, to explore and integrate the real NASA data into the project, and to help write and review parts of the code (the code was directed, tested, and integrated by the team). The AI tutor inside the app uses Google Gemini, with content-safety filters set to the strictest level for minors. The AI-generated audio is acknowledged here and in the audio files’ metadata. No NASA logos or branding were used; this is an independent project, not endorsed by NASA.
